lesson.title: Friendly Numbers: Zero, One Half, and One

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Think about your water bottle at soccer practice at the park. When your coach asks how much you have left, you don't say 'four hundred and thirty seven millilitres.' You just say 'about half.' That word 'half' is a friendly number that helps you talk about amounts quickly. In math we call these friendly numbers benchmarks.

visual.caption: About half the bottle is left

steps.say: Our three favourite benchmarks live on a number line between zero and one. Zero means nothing at all, one half sits right in the middle, and one means a whole. Every fraction and every decimal between zero and one has to snuggle up near one of these three friends. And here is a handy fact to remember: one half and zero point five are exactly the same amount.

Now, how do you know if a fraction is near one half? Here's my little trick: cut the bottom number in half. Take five eighths. Half of eight is four, so four eighths is exactly one half. We have five parts, and five is one more than four, so five eighths is a little bit more than half. Look at the two bars — the bottom one sticks out just a bit.

visual.caption: Four eighths is half; five eighths is a bit more

steps.say: Decimals work the same way, and money makes it easy. Fifty cents out of a whole dollar is half a dollar. So zero point five is our halfway mark. Here is a grid of one hundred little squares, and I have shaded forty eight of them for zero point four eight. Forty eight is just under fifty, so zero point four eight is a tiny bit less than half.

visual.caption: Forty eight hundredths — just under half

steps.say: Let's try one together. Your pizza at family night is cut into twelve slices, and seven slices are gone. Is that closest to zero, to one half, or to one whole? Half of twelve is six, so six twelfths would be exactly half. We have seven, which is only one more slice than six. So seven twelfths is just a smidge over half — the closest benchmark is one half.

visual.caption: Seven of twelve slices — just past half

steps.say: Here's a slightly bigger one. You walk four ninths of a kilometre to the bus stop, then zero point five two of a kilometre from the bus to school. About how far did you walk? Half of nine is four and a half, so four ninths is a little under half. And zero point five two is a little over half. About half plus about half makes about one. So you walked roughly one kilometre. The exact answer is zero point nine six four kilometres — see how close our estimate was?

visual.caption: Start near half, jump about half, land near one

steps.say: Benchmarks also help you put numbers in order without any hard work. Look at zero point three, five eighths, and zero point nine five. Zero point three is below half, five eighths is just above half, and zero point nine five is almost a whole. So from smallest to biggest they go zero point three, then five eighths, then zero point nine five. If you check, five eighths equals zero point six two five, so our order is exactly right.

visual.caption: Below half, just over half, almost one

steps.say: So remember, sweetheart: you don't always need the exact number. Ask yourself, is it near zero, near one half, or near one whole? That one question makes comparing, ordering, and estimating fractions and decimals feel easy.

lesson.answer: Ask 'is it near zero, near one half, or near one whole?' — benchmarks turn tricky fractions and decimals into easy ones.

practice.question: At the grocery store in Kelowna, your bag of carrots weighs 0.48 kilograms and your bag of apples weighs five eighths of a kilogram. Use benchmarks to estimate the total weight, then find the exact total.
practice.answer: Zero point four eight is about one half, and five eighths is a little over one half, so the estimate is about 1 kilogram. Exactly: 0.48 + 0.625 = 1.105 kilograms — just over 1 kilogram, so the estimate was spot on.
